turns.user: my sourdough keeps coming out dense and flat even though my starter doubles in about 4 hours. why does this happen? i get that the starter is working, so I want to understand the actual mechanism of why the loaf still doesn't rise
turns.assistant: A starter that doubles tells you the yeast and bacteria are active, but it doesn't guarantee the dough will rise well. The rise in the loaf comes from gas trapped in a strong gluten network. If the dough is underproofed or overproofed, the gas either hasn't formed enough or has escaped and the structure has weakened. Dense, flat loaves usually point to a problem with bulk fermentation or with gluten development. Under-kneading or too little stretch and fold leaves the network weak, so it can't hold the gas. Too much hydration or cold dough can slow fermentation so the yeast never builds enough pressure. Look at how much the dough itself rose during bulk, not just the starter, and check the windowpane test before shaping.

turns.user: I need to pull citation years out of text. Examples: 'Smith et al. (2019)' and '(Jones, 2004a)' and '(Lee and Park, 2011; Kim 2015)'. My first try grabbed too much, it matched the whole parenthetical. Ideas for patterns?
turns.assistant: A few approaches, depending on how much structure you want. Simplest: match four digits that look like a year with \b(19|20)\d{2}[a-z]?\b. That catches 2019, 2004a and 2015 in your examples, and the word boundary stops it from grabbing longer numbers. Second option: match only inside parentheses with a lookbehind, like (?<=\()[^)]*(?=\)), then extract the years from that. That keeps the author and year together, which helps if you need to pair them. Third option: match the author name and the year as one pattern, such as [A-Z][a-z]+(?: et al\.| and [A-Z][a-z]+)?,? \(?((?:19|20)\d{2}[a-z]?)\)?. That's more complex and breaks on unusual names, so test it on a sample before you rely on it.

turns.user: The first option is too loose, it grabs page numbers sometimes. What about the second one but only the year part
turns.assistant: Use the parenthesized match and then pull the year inside it. Something like: first match the parenthetical with \(([^)]*)\), then inside that group search for (?:19|20)\d{2}[a-z]? and collect the matches. That avoids page numbers like pp. 1995 since you're only searching within citations. If you're in Python, re.findall on the group works well. For '(Lee and Park, 2011; Kim 2015)' you'll get both years, and the page-number problem goes away because page numbers usually appear after a colon or a 'p.' that you can exclude explicitly if you need to.

turns.user: why does my query with a LEFT JOIN still return the same rows as an inner join? i put a WHERE on the right table's column
turns.assistant: Because the WHERE condition filters out the rows where the right table has no match. A LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table, filling the right side with NULLs when there's no match. But if you add WHERE right_table.column = 'something', then NULL rows fail that condition and get removed, so the result behaves like an inner join. The fix is to move the condition into the ON clause if you want to keep unmatched rows, or to keep it in WHERE if you really do want only matched rows.

turns.user: so if i put the condition in the ON clause it keeps all the left rows?
turns.assistant: Yes. When the filter is in the ON clause, the join only matches rows where the right table meets the condition, and every left row still appears. Any left row with no qualifying match gets NULLs for the right table's columns. For example, SELECT c.name, o.total FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid' keeps every customer, while the same status filter in WHERE would drop customers with no paid orders.

turns.user: why do people roll clothes instead of folding them when packing? is it actually better or is it just a meme
turns.assistant: It's partly a real effect and partly overhyped. Rolling works well for casual clothes like t-shirts, shorts, and knits because it reduces the number of hard creases and fits more into a bag, since you're filling small gaps. It also makes it easier to see what you've packed. Folding is usually better for structured items like button-up shirts, blazers, and trousers, since rolled dress clothes can wrinkle in odd places. Most people end up using a mix, rolling soft items and folding the rest, and the difference is smaller than the internet suggests.

turns.user: ok and does rolling actually save space in a backpack vs a suitcase

In a hard-shell suitcase, the walls already define the space, so rolling gains you less, though it can still help with bulk. In either case, the bigger space saver is choosing fewer items and using packing cubes to compress them. Rolling tends to pair well with a backpack because the rolled items can slot around the edges and the bag holds its shape.
